newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Interest rate fears hurt dollar, euro stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Interest rate fears hurt dollar, euro stocks.

text.p: Interest rate uncertainty loomed over financial markets on Tuesday, sending the dollar to five-month lows against the yen and causing sharp drops in European stocks.

Currency markets were suddenly hit by worries that Japan might increase rates, making dollar-denominated assets less attractive to investors, while at the same time European equity investors fretted that U.S. rates were about to go up and sold stock.

The dollar, which strengthened on Monday, reversed direction and fell by nearly four yen overnight in Asia after reports that a committee of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Partly (LDP) was considering asking for higher discount rates from the Bank of Japan.

Japan's domestic media reported that the LDP would recommend an increase in the record low rate of 0.5 percent to keep capital from flowing out of the country following liberalisation of foreign exchange laws.

Japanese financial authorities later moved to halt the dollar's fall, warning that the yen's rise was too rapid. The move helped to push the dollar back over 113 yen, still over two yen below the levels in late Europe on Monday.

But currency traders -- unlike their equity colleagues-- also detected a shift of mood in Washington's commitment to a strong dollar before a meeting of U.S. central bank policy-makers in the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) later on Tuesday.

They cited comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin as evidence of Washington's change in tune. Rubin said the U.S. policy on the dollar remained unchanged -- but did not explicitly repeat his past support for a strong dollar.
The dollar, which struggled to reach 113.60 yen by midday in Europe, has been spiralling downward since hitting a 56-month peak of 127.47 on May 1. Against the mark, it was down nearly two pfennigs

"Rubin's accumulated comments, the possibility the LDP will push for higher rates and the absence of any comments by the Japanese to halt the move...all helped the move," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.

The change of mood contrasted with trade on Monday where the dollar strengthened as investors bet on an increase in rates to come out of the FOMC. A decision was not expected before 1815 GMT, after European markets close.
Uncertainty over U.S. rates also loomed over European bourses. Frankfurt and Paris fell by over 1.5 percent as markets counted the extra cost of doing business.
Frankfurt suffered the most, with floor trade down 1.86 percent at one point as the weaker dollar also hit exporting sectors. Many investors took up defensive positions before the FOMC.
"Due to conflicting U.S. economic data, it is completely open as to if U.S. rates will be increased," a trader said.
In Paris, the blue-chip CAC-40 index fell 1.4 percent by lunchtime, with the market divided over no-change or a quarter percentage point rise in U.S. interest rates.

"We're coming up to a couple of key events -- the FOMC meeting, the French (parliamentary) election -- and the market's at record highs. It's normal to correct," one trader said. The CAC index rose 5.71 percent last week.
London slipped only 0.3 percent, relieved that Wall Street had put in a strong performance overnight, where the Dow added nearly half a percent, but cautious before the FOMC.
"The market looks set to continue drifting off," said one dealer. "But there's no real selling pressure, it's just nerves ahead of the FOMC."
STOCK PRICES AT 1100 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was down 27.1 points at 4,618.1.
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 37.15 points at 2,747.13.
Frankfurt's DAX index was down 59.61 points at 3,544.94.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6969 marks and 113.60 yen compared with 1.7105 marks and 116.09 yen in late European trade on Monday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $342.50 an ounce, compared with Monday's close in London of $341.25. Silver was at $4.72, up three cents.
